claims.claim_text: Effective design for manufacturing depends on the designer having visibility into the specific assembly equipment that will build the board, so that the layout and bill of materials are optimised around what that particular assembler can actually do.
claims.quote_verbatim: you as a designer have got to know what is on those machines
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: Where a fabricator's cheapest process class is known, designing to it rather than to the finest capability available keeps a board in the low-cost tier; a designer whose regular fab quoted six-thousandths-of-an-inch minimum track and gap standardised all small boards on 6/6 for that reason.
claims.quote_verbatim: I knew that they would do 6-6 minimum, so I went and I, you know, I will now do all my board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: Specifying parts an assembly house already keeps loaded on its feeders or holds in stock can be cheaper overall than specifying a nominally cheaper part, because it avoids feeder changes and procurement effort; the saving justifies a slightly higher unit price on the component itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: it pays to use that, pays to design that in, even if it might cost a little bit more
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: Component pricing does not keep halving with each order-of-magnitude increase in quantity. A jump from single units to a hundred can roughly halve the price, but a further jump to a thousand generally does not repeat that saving except on generic jellybean parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you've got those jelly bean generic parts
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Part selection during design should be made against volume price breaks rather than single-unit prices, even when only prototypes are being built, because the chosen parts are difficult to change once the design is frozen.
claims.quote_verbatim: you really should be looking at those large volume prices anyway, even if you're just planning on building a couple of them for now
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The turnkey contract manufacturer's role extends beyond assembly into completing the design, including redesigning portions of it for manufacturability and producing the enclosure, so that a customer can hand over a hand-built prototype and receive finished units.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of CMs you can give half-baked products to, and they'll finish a remarkable part of the design
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Catalogue distributors list every part but give no indication of which parts are commonly used or available at manufacturing scale, so a bill of materials assembled purely from distributor part numbers can be unbuildable or expensive in a factory's local supply ecosystem.
claims.quote_verbatim: which of these parts is common and which of these parts is going to be available on a large scale for manufacturing
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Substituting a locally standard component for a rarely used equivalent can cut that line item to roughly a tenth of its cost, which is why factories routinely return a submitted parts list with alternates drawn from what is common in their own market.
claims.quote_verbatim: use this other standard diode that everybody has access to and it'll be like a tenth of the cost
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: Designing next to where the product is built exposes problems invisible on paper, such as a component that consistently falls off the board or an enclosure whose assembly takes three and a half hours where a single change would reduce it to half an hour.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe I need to redesign this mechanical enclosure, because it takes three and a half hours to assemble it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: SpaceX, Enclosures & Startups - Urging Unemployment Ullagone

claims.claim_text: A design constrained from the outset to hand-solderable geometry, with 0603 passives and no package finer than SSOP, needs little preparation before it can be machine assembled, because every such limit is looser than what a pick-and-place line requires.
claims.quote_verbatim: we use 0603 size and no chips smaller than SSOP and fairly hand solderable friendly stuff, we don't have to do a lot of DFM
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: An unexplained jump in an assembly quote often traces to sourcing: rather than substitute, the factory imported the exact specified part and paid duties on it. Specifying generic parts, or explicitly authorising local equivalents, prevents this.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were worried that the part they could source locally wasn't good enough. And so they went ahead and sourced from the US and then it costs more than expected
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Designing from a standard in-house part library, and quoting against that library rather than against specific manufacturer part numbers, lets an assembler stock a single set of parts that covers every board in the product line and shortens procurement.
claims.quote_verbatim: We also design according to a standard part list now.
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Non-recurring engineering cost is roughly flat between a thousand and a hundred thousand units, so the volume a product is designed for changes the design itself far more than it changes the up-front engineering charge; a large swing in expected orders can force substantial redesign.
claims.quote_verbatim: The difference between NRE for manufacturing a thousand units versus a hundred thousand units is not much.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: A machined feature that cannot be reached on a two-axis machine forces the job onto a five-axis machine at substantially higher cost, so the axis count of the intended machine is a design constraint rather than a shop-floor detail.
claims.quote_verbatim: not on this two axis machine. I need a five axis, but then that costs a lot more
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Placement machine setup is quantised by feeder count: a board with one more unique part than the machine has feeder slots forces a second setup pass, which is why unique part count, not total placement count, drives assembly setup cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have 20 feeders and you put 21 parts on a board, you have to redo your setup
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Minimising the number of unique parts on a board is a core design-for-manufacturing lever, and a typical machine setup charge for a small board runs around 250 dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want to minimize your part count because that helps lower your overall cost
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Injection-moulding design guidelines such as permissible draft angle are tiered by mould budget: cheap tooling imposes the most conservative rules, expensive tooling relaxes them, and only operations running very high volume tooling can attempt geometries that are otherwise impossible.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're running really cheap molds, you can have this draft angle and a bunch of guidelines. If you're expensive, you can do this.
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Testability work can be moved earlier in the design cycle by routing test access through a JTAG chain or onto silicon, which reduces the number of physical test points a board needs; the physical handling, fixturing and probing of boards through the production line remains regardless.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe you move it all to be on a JTAG chain, right? So maybe you don't need as many test points
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Hardware has no equivalent of recompiling, so the design entering production must be correct; from completed design-for-manufacturing work and a hundred verification units, reaching very large quantity fulfilment typically takes up to eighteen months rather than the one to three months backers are often promised.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to be perfect when you go to production
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: An electronics manufacturing services provider handed a design will often re-engineer circuit topologies for cost, for example replacing a switching regulator with a linear one where the additional power loss is tolerable, because saving twenty cents on the bill of materials is significant at consumer volumes.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can get away with not having a buck converter and you can just have a simple linear regulator
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: An automated board service can interpose a design-for-manufacturing layer that inspects an uploaded design and rejects the order outright when the design would fail, rather than accepting it and building a board that cannot work.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you upload something that's going to cause you to shoot your toes off, we're going to bounce
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: A fabricator should not silently alter a customer's copper, for instance by widening traces, because the design of record then diverges from what was built; corrections belong in the designer's own files.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want to be fixing your design at the board house
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Automated test and handling equipment is built around a fixed board geometry: custom trays, pneumatic ejectors and bed-of-nails fixtures all assume the board's size and test-point positions, so moving a test point or changing board dimensions invalidates the fixturing investment.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you change the size of your board all all of your cartridge handling systems change
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Assemblers routinely flag vias placed in a QFN's thermal pad area before build, because the via draws solder away during reflow; changes of this kind are identified in the contract manufacturer's design review rather than by the designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: in your QFN you have these, you know, like buried vias or whatever. This is gonna have a bad time
claims.speaker: Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: General-purpose mechanical CAD packages do not check whether a modelled part can actually be machined, so an inexperienced designer discovers unmachinable features only through repeated iterations with the shop.
claims.quote_verbatim: So how do I know that I'm doing something wrong? I'd have to go back and forth with the machine shop 20 times
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A quick manual test for machinability is to imagine the cutting tool as a pencil held perpendicular to the part and to trace how each feature would be reached; anything that cannot be reached that way needs a tilted head or a machine with more axes.
claims.quote_verbatim: think about it like holding a pencil and think about how you would make that part
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: A company masters production by being present on the line, designing its own assembly and test fixtures, handing them to the contract manufacturer and iterating on them, rather than delegating the whole process to a large supplier.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to design the fixture that makes this process more efficient. Uh, and I'm going to give it to the CM so they know how to use it.
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: An assembler prices a difficult board with a risk premium rather than a cost increase: the run may go through cleanly and simply return higher margin, but the probability of rework and scrap is what the surcharge covers.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're going to have to charge more for this assembly
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Solder paste deposition sets a practical floor on component size: below a certain size jet printing is no longer usable and a stencil is required, and very small apertures demand an expensive stencil, so shrinking passives raises assembly cost as well as risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: the smaller, the component, the more difficult it is to print solder paste, right? You can't use a jet printer. You got to use a stencil
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: A part must be designed for the process that will make it, since the geometry suited to additive printing differs from that suited to sheet-metal bending or turning; a designer unaware of the available processes produces generic curved shapes that suit none of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't know what's out there, then you're going to design a thing that's just generic and curvy
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The minimum via size a fabricator will accept follows directly from the fact that the hole is mechanically drilled, so the smallest available drill bit sets the limit; seeing the drilling step performed makes the rule self-evident.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you make them too small, they like can't use a drill bit anymore
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Volume products reserve internal clearance for the battery to swell as it ages, because a predictable fraction of the fleet will show expansion; consuming that allowance to fit extra hardware is acceptable in a one-off but would cause field failures across a production run.
claims.quote_verbatim: I used up a lot of the extra space that Apple had, um, allocated for the battery to expand
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Custom mechanical parts should be designed so they can be produced by a prototype-compatible process as well as the production one: a heatsink destined for die casting should still be machinable, and an enclosure destined for injection moulding should still be printable, so prototypes can be built before tooling exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: make sure you design it so that it is machinable
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A design-for-manufacturing review on a mechanical part at consumer scale produces a report of roughly twenty pages, worked through line by line with the supplier over hours of calls; this is engineering work, not a project management task.
claims.quote_verbatim: get on the phone with a diecast supplier for three hours in the evenings and like scrub through like a 20 page DFM report
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: For moulded plastic parts the decisive threshold is the cutting of tooling steel: design changes must be made before the mould is cut, because afterwards they mean modifying or replacing the tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's so much easier to fix it before you've cut a mold. Like before you start cutting steel
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: A prototype optimised for hand assembly, local sourcing and printing is effectively a different design from the production version, so schedule and iteration must be budgeted for the transition, including several runs with the real suppliers to find and fix issues.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't expect that the version that you prototyped is going to be the same version that you go to production with
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Design for manufacturing cannot be performed alone from published best practice; on a moulded part it consists of an extended exchange with the supplier about what they can and cannot do and what their mould flow analysis shows, which on a complex product can run for months before tooling is ordered.
claims.quote_verbatim: DFM is not something that you can do in a vacuum
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Choosing a fabrication process to match the geometry matters more than defaulting to the most flexible one: a folded sheet-plastic part made over a heated nichrome wire is straightforward, while printing the same shape struggles with undercuts and thin walls.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going to have a terrible time with all the undercuts
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Connector pin assignment should leave spare pins as margin between high-voltage supply pins and low-voltage data and ground pins, so that moisture ingress bridging adjacent contacts does not put the supply directly onto signal lines.
claims.quote_verbatim: they could have left a couple of spare pins between there and not had the, you know, the data and ground pins right next to the high voltage DC thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Teardown comparisons of a Tesla against established volume car makers found substantially more fasteners for the same function, for example five bolts where Toyota used two, attributed to designers without experience of designing for low-cost volume production; the consequence appears as production cost and throughput problems.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're using five bolts here when Toyota are only using two
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Through-hole pins soldered by a selective soldering machine need a clear area around them on the underside of the board, on the order of ten millimetres, because the selective solder head cannot reach a pin surrounded by surface-mount parts; violating the keep-out forces the joints to be hand soldered at much higher cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: don't put your surface mount parts on the bottom of the board close to within like 10 millimeters of your through hole pins
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Visiting several comparable factories, rather than one, is what establishes a designer's sense of what is normal and what is unusual for a process, and watching parts being made leads directly to better designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: Unless you visited the factory and ideally visited a bunch of similar factories, you don't know what's normal.
claims.speaker: Jesse Vincent

claims.claim_text: A factory reviewing a finished design frequently identifies trivial changes, such as reorienting a component or shifting it, that would have removed several dollars of unit cost had they been made during layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: turn a resistor or they, you know, move something to the side or whatever, they're like, you know, you would have saved five bucks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Multiplying per-board component counts by planned annual volume exposes availability limits early: fifty LEDs on each of fifty thousand boards is two and a half million parts, a quantity few sources hold, with lead times of at least twenty weeks that must be built into the schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is going to be a very specific lead time. It's at least 20 weeks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Committing to a long-lead part at volume locks the design to it, so an engineering shortfall found later, such as inadequate thermal testing, cannot be fixed by substitution without writing off the parts already ordered.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can't change that part now because no, we've, we've already ordered, you know, half a million parts
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Bare-board cost falls with layer count, so escaping a ball grid array's pins on four layers rather than six is worth pursuing where the routing allows it.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can escape your BGA on four layers, you do it because it's going to be cheaper
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Fabricators price by process class, so relaxing a design from three-thousandths track and space to four moves it into a cheaper class and widens the set of fabs that can build it; designing to the finest available geometry as a point of pride removes that option.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lower quality process technology, like a 4,000, 4,000 instead of 3,000, 3,000 track space
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Buying a fine-pitch subsystem as a module confines the tight tolerances to a small board built by someone else, and the module often arrives pre-certified for radio compliance, at the price of a higher unit cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is why modules are a good idea sometimes too
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Board houses have exposed their internal incoming-inspection checks as self-service web tools that accept uploaded Gerbers and a bill of materials and return a manufacturability assessment with a visualiser, removing the need to route a simple quote through a sales engineer.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have a fantastic DFM tool. So you go upload your Gerbers on there.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The threshold for moving production overseas is better judged by annual revenue than by unit count, since an expensive product justifies the supply chain at low volume; one contract manufacturer put its own threshold at a million dollars a year, low relative to the tier-one houses.
claims.quote_verbatim: our threshold is a million dollars a year
claims.speaker: Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: Increasing a moulded part's draft angle from two to three degrees lets the part release from the tool faster and raises yield, with no functional or aesthetic consequence, which is the kind of change a moulding or machining shop will identify in minutes.
claims.quote_verbatim: can you change this draft angle from like 2% to 3% because we'll be able to release it faster
claims.speaker: Michael Corr
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Withholding CAD files from the manufacturing partner until after internal design review delays their feedback until the design is frozen; a five-minute change identified at that point cost two weeks of schedule that could not be recovered.
claims.quote_verbatim: we didn't give a copy of the CAD file, the step file to our CNC shop until it was already been designed and already been through our review process
claims.speaker: Michael Corr
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: A cost-down pass during design for manufacturing typically has the contract manufacturer propose substitutes from its local supply ecosystem, which the designer then evaluates and approves; this is how designs prototyped with locally available parts end up populated with regional brands.
claims.quote_verbatim: the CM's like, hey, we want to replace them with all these much lower cost chips. You do an eval
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A component repeated hundreds of times dominates a bill of materials, so its unit cost effectively sets the product price; a calendar product with one mechanical switch per day of the year would have reached roughly fifteen hundred dollars retail.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you have 365 of everything or of anything on a bomb, like the cost of that unit is going to heavily implicate the cost of the, of the product as a whole
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: Replacing hundreds of mechanical inputs with capacitive touch pads etched into the board removes the dominant bill-of-materials cost and the associated assembly labour, at the price of a very large single circuit board serving as the product's front panel.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we ended up using capacitive touch.
claims.speaker: Simone Giertz

claims.claim_text: Hand placing the first boards of a design generates most of its manufacturability insights, because the designer directly experiences the consequences of choices such as an unnecessarily small passive size.
claims.quote_verbatim: the best way to do DFM is to experience the pain of your design decision
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A design can be complete, working and indistinguishable from a finished product while still failing to reach production, because it is manufacturable only at a cost above any viable price point.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not really manufacturable let's say well it is but not cheaply at a price point that would
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Mismatches between the ordered component package and the footprint placed on the board, such as 0805 parts against 0402 land patterns, are a routine finding in a first design-for-manufacturing report and are caught before build rather than at assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: parts that have 0805 in the name do not fit on top of 0402 footprints
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Errors cluster in the final stage of a design, when late manufacturability-driven part substitutions are made under schedule pressure and without review; on one board the last five percent of the work produced the large majority of the mistakes.
claims.quote_verbatim: the last five percent of the design is where i made probably 95 of the errors
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: An enclosure developed as a printed part frequently cannot be produced by the intended volume process, because printing imposes almost none of the constraints that moulding or casting does, and the mismatch surfaces only when the design reaches the production house.
claims.quote_verbatim: you 3d print something. And then when you're finally going to production, the production house says, we can't build this
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Starting a product from an off-the-shelf enclosure and designing the board to fit it removes tooling cost and mechanical risk entirely, and is a common origin for successful small-volume products.
claims.quote_verbatim: you see a case and you go, Ooh, I could make that into a product. That's the perfect form factor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A manufacturability check written by the shop that will cut the part can flag geometry no general CAD package will, such as an internal corner radius smaller than the smallest available router bit, and highlight the offending feature in the model.
claims.quote_verbatim: you cannot manufacture that because the in cutters, you know, the router bit's going to be too small
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Data Provenance in the Home, Server, and Fab

claims.claim_text: Constraining a design to a fixed personal part library, in the way a printed part is designed around print orientation, allows boards to be iterated on in-house without feeder changes; the constraint is tighter than a contract manufacturer would impose but is chosen deliberately for speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: Can I only design boards with this set of parts?
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Automated manufacturability checking covers simple two- and four-layer boards without human involvement, but the number of possible combinations of via structures, track and gap, and stackups grows so large on complex boards that human review is still required.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's a simple two four layer board, that stuff generally is not touched by a human
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Manufacturing constraints ideally belong inside the design tool rather than in the fabricator's checking stage, following semiconductor practice where the fab publishes a process design kit expressing its rules as executable code rather than as a specification sheet for the designer to transcribe.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want most of those design constraints in the tool ultimately
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: The correct trade between design time and unit cost follows volume: at five million units, several days of engineering to remove ten cents of cost pays for itself many times over.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're going to make 5 million units or something, you probably want to trade your design time for your production cost
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Most electronics designs are industrial or medical products built in the low thousands, where optimising for manufacturing cost is the wrong objective and accessibility, reworkability and robustness of the design matter more.
claims.quote_verbatim: the correct trade in that circumstance is often not to optimize for manufacturing costs
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: A bill-of-materials export checked before release against the assembler's own catalogue and stock levels acts as a lightweight manufacturability review, flagging parts the assembler does not stock and which will therefore carry a sourcing surcharge.
claims.quote_verbatim: this doesn't have a, you know, an LCSC component. And then, you know, there's going to be extra cost as a result of that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Components falling off the first side of a double-sided board during the second reflow pass is a predictable failure, and it is prevented at the design review stage by checking part mass and placement against the second-pass profile rather than by adjusting the process.
claims.quote_verbatim: no, but that's because we do the DFM review
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: A design-for-manufacture review performed before a board is released checks clearance between parts for the pick-and-place head to reach, spacing between adjacent components, and which side of the board each part sits on, and may require the board to be laid out again.
claims.quote_verbatim: Is there, is there clearance between the parts so that the pick and place head, are they too close together?
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: At quantities of ten or twenty an assembler can absorb a poor layout with custom jigging and manual intervention, but by a few hundred units the process must run unattended, so design faults that were merely inconvenient become the limiting cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're doing like 10 or 20 or something, we can, we can jig it together and make it work. But if you're doing like 500 or something, DFM plays a bigger role.
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: Selecting a layer stackup from a fabricator's published standard set, rather than specifying an arbitrary one, avoids a custom quote and its cost and lead-time penalty; comparing available stackups and prices across several fabs to find where the cost curve bends is a routine part of the work.
claims.quote_verbatim: Maybe you're going to do one of the JLC standard stack ups.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
